name: Flow (GRAIL-B)
intro: Flow was Ebb’s twin. For almost a year it followed Ebb around the Moon, and in the end it followed Ebb down too, hitting the same mountain about 20 seconds later. NASA named the crash site after Sally Ride, the first American woman in space. Look up: a see-through copy of Flow hangs over its crater, just as it looked a moment before impact, with more spots in the sky around it.
whyLeft: With fuel nearly gone and its orbit dropping, Flow was steered into a remote mountain so it could never fall onto a historic landing site.
repurpose: The Sally K. Ride Impact Site could be a memorial stop for future explorers, honouring the astronaut who led the twins’ student camera program.
funFact: Flow and Ebb each carried a MoonKAM camera run for students: middle school classes chose spots on the Moon for the cameras to photograph.

hotspots.title: Flow’s crater
hotspots.text: Flow hit the same mountainside just a short distance from Ebb’s crater. From orbit, its crater looks like a tiny dark dot.

photo.alt: An orbital view of a slope with a small new crater
photo.caption: Flow’s impact crater, photographed by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter after the crash.
photo.licenseEvidence: LROC images (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University) are free for educational use with credit; this site is an educational NASA Space Apps project.

hotspots.title: Sally Ride Impact Site
hotspots.text: NASA named this spot the Sally K. Ride Impact Site. Sally Ride led MoonKAM, the cameras on the twins that let thousands of students take their own pictures of the Moon.

source.label: NASA JPL: GRAIL impact site named for Sally Ride

hotspots.title: Ebb’s crater
hotspots.text: Ebb’s crater is nearby. The twins flew in a line about 175 to 225 km apart while mapping gravity, and stayed together right to the end.

photo.alt: Two orbital views side by side showing the two small GRAIL impact craters
photo.caption: Both GRAIL impact craters, Ebb’s and Flow’s, photographed by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.
photo.licenseEvidence: LROC images (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University) are free for educational use with credit; this site is an educational NASA Space Apps project.

hotspots.title: Empty tanks
hotspots.text: Flow ran its engine until the fuel was gone, then coasted into the mountain. Scout, no repair is possible: the spacecraft was broken into fragments by the impact.

source.label: NASA JPL: GRAIL impact site named for Sally Ride

hotspots.title: Link to Ebb
hotspots.text: Flow flew behind Ebb, and this horn kept a radio link aimed at its twin. When Ebb passed over a mountain or a heavy patch of rock, the Moon’s pull tugged it ahead a little, and the link caught the change.

hotspots.title: Star tracker
hotspots.text: This little telescope read the stars to tell Flow which way it was pointing, so its radio horn could stay aimed at Ebb.

hotspots.title: The slow road
hotspots.text: Its solar panels kept Flow powered through a long, fuel-saving trip. It left Earth on 10 September 2011 and slipped into orbit around the Moon at New Year, about 25 hours after Ebb.

source.label: NASA: GRAIL impact sites, craters about 5 m with dark ejecta (depth estimated)
